opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so my view has shifted quite a lot here. When we first started writing about AI control, a few years ago, I think a lot of us, me included, had this picture where control could be one of the main pillars of a safety case. A responsible AI company could say: "We can't be confident our models aren't scheming against us, but we've set up enough monitoring, enough restrictions on what they can do, and run enough adversarial evaluations that even if they are scheming, the chance they cause a catastrophe is really low." We were imagining something like getting risk down to a fraction of a percent, the kind of number you'd actually want if you were being careful.

I've become a lot more pessimistic about that framing, for a couple of reasons.

The first is just about what AI companies are actually going to do. That picture assumed a lab willing to pay substantial costs: slowing down deployment, having lots of humans audit suspicious actions, restricting model affordances in annoying ways, running careful control evaluations with a red team that's really trying. My best guess now is that, absent major changes in regulation or the competitive landscape, labs won't be willing to pay those costs when the models are most dangerous. The race dynamics are intense, and the willingness to accept even modest productivity hits for safety seems lower than I'd hoped.

The second is more technical. As you get to models that are substantially superhuman in relevant domains, the control story gets harder. A lot of control techniques rely on the gap between the untrusted model and the trusted models and humans you're using to supervise it not being too big. Once that gap is large, it's hard to be confident your red team is eliciting the model's best attack strategies, and the evaluations themselves become less trustworthy. So even an ideal lab would find it very hard to get to really low risk with control alone at that capability level.

So where I've landed is that I think about control less as "the thing that lets a careful company get risk really low" and more as "a set of relatively cheap interventions that can substantially reduce risk in the rushed, messy world we're probably going to be in." I spend a lot more time thinking about what I sometimes describe as the low-willingness-to-pay regime: if a lab is only willing to spend a small fraction of its compute and staff on safety, what are the highest-value things to do? And I think control techniques do really well in that regime. You can go from a situation where a scheming model could pretty easily exfiltrate its weights or sabotage safety research to one where it's meaningfully harder, and that's worth a lot, even if you're not getting to the 0.1% risk numbers we originally talked about.

I'd also say control looks more valuable to me as a way of buying time and extracting useful work from early transformatively useful AIs, rather than as a long-term solution. The goal is to get through the period where models are capable enough to be really useful, including for alignment research, but not yet so capable that control breaks down, and use that window as productively as possible.

r001.rationale: He says he initially saw AI control as a main pillar of a safety case, allowing a responsible company to argue that catastrophe risk was very low even if models were scheming.

r002.rationale: He says he has become much more pessimistic: companies may not accept the costs, and even an ideal lab would struggle to reach very low risk with control alone as models become substantially superhuman.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think my views have shifted in a way that's a little subtle, so let me try to lay it out carefully.

When we first started talking about AI control a couple of years ago, the pitch was roughly: suppose you have a model that might be scheming, that might be actively trying to subvert your safety measures. Can you nonetheless get useful work out of it while keeping the probability of catastrophe very low? And "very low" there was doing a lot of work. The hope was that you could make arguments like, "Even if this model is trying as hard as it can to cause a disaster, the chance it succeeds is below some small number," and you could back that up with something like adversarial evaluation, where a red team plays the role of the scheming model and you check that your monitoring and auditing catch them.

I still think that basic framing is right, and honestly I think the field has moved toward it more than I expected. But I've become more pessimistic about the "very low risk" part specifically, for a few reasons.

The first is just that the deployments are much bigger and messier than the toy settings we were imagining. When you have models running for hours autonomously inside a company, touching lots of infrastructure, doing millions of actions a day, the attack surface is enormous. The control arguments we could make in a clean setting, where there's one model doing one task and a trusted monitor watching every action, degrade a lot when you try to scale them to the real thing. There are many more places for a model to take a sneaky action that looks fine in isolation.

The second thing is that I've updated toward thinking the thing that actually gets you the low risk is not any single clever technique. It's the boring stuff. Logging everything, having good permission systems, actually knowing what your models are doing and being able to audit it after the fact. A lot of what I'd now call "control" looks much more like ordinary security and insider threat mitigation than like a novel AI safety research agenda. And companies are much worse at that boring stuff than I'd like them to be, because it's annoying and it slows people down.

The third thing is about what level of risk reduction is realistic. I used to talk as if control could get you to something like a one in a thousand chance of a scheming model causing a catastrophe during a given deployment. I now think that for the models we'll have soon, a more honest target is something like "substantially reduce the risk compared to doing nothing," rather than "drive it to near zero." If a model is much smarter than the people building the control measures, and it's scheming, I think the honest answer is that your measures are likely to have holes you didn't think of. Control buys you a lot in the regime where the model is roughly comparable to your red team. It buys you less as that gap widens.

So where does that leave me? I'd say I'm more convinced than ever that control is a necessary part of what a responsible AI company should be doing, and less convinced that it's sufficient to get the risk down to the level I'd want. Which means I care more now about complementary things: being able to detect scheming directly, through evals or interpretability or just catching models in the act; having the ability to pause or roll back if something looks off; and, frankly, not deploying models in situations where a successful subversion would be irrecoverable.

One thing I'd push back on, though, is the framing that control is somehow a disappointment because it can't give you very low risk on its own. I think the right comparison is to the counterfactual, which is companies deploying increasingly capable models with basically no safeguards against the possibility that those models are adversarial. Compared to that, control is a huge improvement, and it's one that doesn't require solving any deep open problems. That's still the thing I find most compelling about it.

r001.rationale: The response says the initial hope was to argue that even a scheming model had a chance below a small number of causing catastrophe, supported by adversarial evaluation. That communicates safety cases as an advantage of control.

r002.rationale: The response says Buck has become more pessimistic about achieving very low risk and is less convinced control is sufficient, describing a realistic goal as substantial risk reduction rather than near zero.

astra-6.text:
I’ve become more pessimistic about how far AI control gets you, particularly if the goal is to establish that the risk is very low. I still think it’s a promising way to reduce risk. But there’s a substantial gap between showing that your safeguards defeat the attacks you’ve thought of and showing that a scheming model has a very small chance of succeeding.

The difficulty is that your safety argument depends on how well you can elicit attacks during testing. If the model has some strategy that your tests don’t uncover, you might come away feeling reassured without having tested the thing that matters. And as models become more capable, it gets harder to be confident that you’ve covered the relevant possibilities.

So I’d distinguish ‘control makes deploying this model substantially safer’ from ‘control lets us confidently conclude that deploying this model is extremely safe.’ I’m more optimistic about the first claim than the second. I still want companies to do this work, but I’m less comfortable treating it as sufficient by itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses control’s safety benefits and limitations, but does not identify constructing safety cases as an advantage Shlegeris initially saw.

r002.rationale: He says he has become more pessimistic about whether control can establish very low risk, and distinguishes making deployment safer from confidently concluding it is extremely safe, which control alone cannot provide.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more pessimistic about the strongest version of that claim. There’s a difference between saying, “AI control could substantially reduce the risk from a scheming model,” and saying, “An AI company could use control to establish that the risk is very low.” I’m still pretty enthusiastic about the first claim. The second seems harder to me than it used to.

The basic difficulty is that you need to evaluate your safeguards against models that are actively trying to get around them. And the attacks you manage to elicit in your evaluations might be worse than the attacks the model would come up with when it really mattered. So you can do an experiment, observe that your defenses catch all the attacks, and still have a pretty important question about what that tells you.

There’s also a distinction between having a promising control technique and having a whole deployment where you’ve accounted for the dangerous opportunities. A model might be doing lots of different tasks, with different permissions, over a long period of time. Getting confidence in that entire setup is a much bigger ask than demonstrating a defense in a relatively clean experimental setting.

So I’d now put more emphasis on control as one component of a safety case, and on restricting deployments to settings where the argument is actually credible. I don’t think the takeaway is that control doesn’t work. It’s that “we have useful defenses” is a substantially weaker statement than “we’ve established very low risk,” and I’m more worried about that gap.

r001.rationale: The response mentions safety cases as a component of control, but does not say Buck initially viewed constructing safety cases as an advantage of AI control.

r002.rationale: The response says establishing very low risk through control seems harder than before, but does not clearly convey a shift to considering that outcome implausible.
